text.p: The rolling terrain of the Augusta National course may keep Jose Maria Olazabal out of next month's U.S. Masters despite a fine return from crippling foot problems at the Desert Classic last week.
The 31-year-old Spaniard exceeded many expectations with his 12th place finish in Dubai on Sunday, his first event after 18 months out of the game.

And while he did not ultimately threaten the leaders in the event won by Australian Richard Green, his nine-under-par 279 from rounds of 69-74-65-71 pleased the former world number four. The performance boosted him to 203rd in the world from the 225th position he held a week earlier.
What made him happiest was that he came through seven days of 18-hole practice, pro-am and tournament rounds with his feet not causing him serious problems.

"I'm not worse than when I came here, which is good news. That is the most positive thing of the week," he said. "I coped with seven rounds pretty well even though I had some problems at the ends of rounds. But I recovered pretty well for the next day."
Olazabal will assess his condition this week before deciding where next he plays, and while Augusta in April has a magnetic attraction for the player who won there in 1994, he is not sure he will go.
"It would be nice but obviously I have to take into consideration that that golf course particularly is killing," he said.
"There is not a single hole that is flat, maybe the 16th. But the rest are up and down. You really get tired on that course."
Olazabal had treatment on his back every day in the physiotherapy van at the Dubai course and said that when he got home from the tournament he would have manipulation of his feet.
This was Olazabal's first event since he played in the Lancome Trophy in 1995. He left there so dispirited from the pain in his feet that he withdrew from that year's European Ryder Cup team.
So began his attempts to recover from a condition that was initially diagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis. For much of last year he could do nothing but rest and hope the problem would just go away.
But it seemed to get worse and by mid-year Olazabal at various times could barely stand, had to crawl from his bedroom to his bathroom and feared that he would be consigned to a wheelchair.

After some improvement, several returns to competition were mooted but all were called off. But a chance meeting during a trip to Germany late last year to get some shoes adjusted led to his introduction to a doctor of alternative medicine, Hans-Wilhelm Muller-Wohlfahrt.
He has treated such athletes as Boris Becker and Daley Thompson in his time and he diagnosed a problem surrounding two bones in Olazabal's back which affected his feet.
He immediately prescribed a course of exercise and physiotherapy, and improvement was swift.
Olazabal started practising again only three weeks before the Dubai event.
While he sorts out his schedule, he admits the pain he still suffers will prevent him from playing four consecutive weeks, as he used to.
His next target will be to see if he can play two weeks in succession, which he may do before the Masters "to know if I'm able to do so."
Meanwhile, there was delight among his fellow European professionals, especially after his third round 65 on Saturday.
As World number one Greg Norman put it, "Once a competitor, always a competitor. It's like riding a bike, you don't forget."
